meaning: The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters

pronunciation.note: Ọba names the river orisha of the Ọba River; the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form (tone marks cannot be registered), and the fuller tone-marked Ọ̀bà is preserved in the temple's display text. The dot-below marks the open-mid vowel.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Ọ̀bà — the river orisha; her name is the river's name, and the river's name is hers

kin.label: Yoruba homonym
kin.form: ọba, 'king, ruler' — a common noun spelled identically; the orisha and the royal title are traditionally distinguished by tone and context

domains.title: The River that Endures
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Jealousy, and the Lake of the Co-Wife
domains.lead: Ọba is the river orisha who loved and lost: the senior wife of Ṣàngó, whose jealousy cost her an ear and whose grief became a lake. She is the Yoruba study of endurance — the quiet river that outlasts the storm-god's louder wives, and whose crown was redesigned to hide, and honor, the wound at once.

cards.name: The Ọba River
cards.desc: Her water in Yorubaland — the stream that bears her name and her temperament, quiet where the storm-wives are loud.

cards.name: The Hidden Ear
cards.desc: The ear she lost to the co-wives' trick — hidden under her crown and her hair, which is why her images never show the ears.

cards.name: The Senior Wife
cards.desc: The first wife of the thunder-king — and the last to be believed when the household turned cruel.

cards.name: The Lake
cards.desc: Her grief made geography: the lake where the faithful still mourn with her, season after season.

symbols.name: The covered ear
symbols.meaning: Wounds hidden and endured — dignity after injury; her images never show the ears

symbols.name: The crown of the hidden ear
symbols.meaning: Regalia redesigned around the wound — the only crown in the corpus that exists to hide and honor at once

symbols.name: The brass bracelet
symbols.meaning: Her marriage-token from the thunder-king, kept after the palace cast her out

symbols.name: The red parrot feather
symbols.meaning: Her sign beside the other wives' red — the household's colors she was never allowed to outshine

symbols.name: The river Ọba
symbols.meaning: Her name made water — the stream in Yorubaland that keeps her longer than any palace could

mythology.lead: Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake. The cycle survives in Yoruba oral tradition — oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Bascom and others — and crossed the Atlantic to become the diaspora's parable of the polygamous household.

myths.title: Three Wives, One Storm
myths.text: Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The cycle survives in the oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Yoruba specialists from the mid-twentieth century — Wande Abimbola's editions of Ifá verse, William Bascom's collections of tales — and in the diaspora the three wives became the standard cast of every household drama. The tellings agree on the shape: Ọba, the first wife, watched her husband's love flow downhill to Ọṣun, and love that is watched curdles into jealousy. In the fullest tellings Ọba schemed against Ọṣun — and Ọṣun, the shrewdest of the household, let the scheme come to her first and answered it with one that would end the rivalry. The seniority that should have protected Ọba is exactly what the story burns: in the thunder-king's house, the first wife is the last to be believed, and the household's peace is purchased with her humiliation.

myths.title: The Ear in the Soup
myths.text: The trap is the cycle's most famous scene, preserved in the folktale collections (Bascom, African Folktales) and endlessly retold in the diaspora. Ọṣun — in some tellings Ọya — let fall that the king loved, above all things, the taste of his beloved's ear in his soup. Ọba, desperate to be loved again, cut off her own ear and cooked it for him. When the bowl came before Ṣàngó and the trick stood revealed, his disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north weeping, her maimed head hidden under her crown and her hair. The sources disagree on which co-wife set the trap and on how much of the truth Ṣàngó ever learned — the oral tradition keeps the variants alive rather than settling them. What every telling keeps is the ear: the organ of obedience, cut off to buy a love that was never for sale. The myth is the Yoruba anatomy of jealousy — not the villain's punishment, but the victim's self-mutilation, and the crown she designed afterward to live with it.

myths.title: The Water of Her Grief
myths.text: Her tears became her realm. In the tellings, Ọba's flight ended in the water that still bears her name: the Ọba River of Yorubaland, and the lake of her worship, where her priests keep her cult and the faithful mourn with her on her appointed days. The geography is the theology — a goddess exiled from the palace takes the river as her palace, and the quiet water outlasts the thunder. The tradition preserves one firm ritual rule from the household war: Ọba and Ọya, the senior wife and the storm-sharer, can never be honored in the same shrine; some quarrels the orisha themselves decline to reconcile. But her people read the ending differently than the palace did: storms pass, the river stays. The senior wife outlasted the storm-god's louder wives by becoming the thing the storm cannot be — permanent, low, and always arriving.

myths.title: Obá Crosses the Water
myths.text: The wives' cycle crossed the Middle Passage with the orisha, and in the Americas it acquired its second life. In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría — whose wheel she shares, and whose feast day, 25 November, became hers; her cult proved strongest in Matanzas province, where her initiates arrange the hair forward over the ears exactly as she arranged hers, the gesture intact across four hundred years and an ocean. In Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, and the three-wives drama remains the standard parable told to explain the polygamous household's wars and survivors. Robert Farris Thompson documented how thoroughly the diaspora kept her iconography — the hidden ear is legible in Lucumí altars from Havana to Miami. The crossing is itself the last episode of the myth: the wife the palace expelled became the orisha the ocean could not drown, carried in the hair of women who had lost everything else and still arranged it, forward, covering, dignified.

lore.syncretism: In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría (Saint Catherine, whose wheel she shares) — her cult strong in Matanzas; in Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, the devotee-dancers' hair arranged to hide what the king did. The three-wife cycle (Ọba-Ọṣun-Ọya) is the diaspora's standard parable of the polygamous household, told wherever the orisha went — and the co-wives' ritual incompatibility, the rule that Ọba and Ọya never share a shrine, was carried across the Atlantic as faithfully as any scripture. Thompson's Flash of the Spirit traces her iconography through Lucumí altars from Havana to Miami: the covered ear is one of the most durable images in the African-Atlantic world, a wound turned into regalia by four centuries of women's hands.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her image — the crowned figure hiding her ears — is one of Yoruba art's most intimate: the wound as regalia. The co-wives' cycle structures the orisha households of two continents; her river in Yorubaland keeps her shrines active; and the 'Obá' of Cuban Santería is beloved as the most patient of the female orisha — the one who teaches that endurance is also a form of power. The brass bracelet of her marriage and the red parrot feather of her household appear in shrine and carnival alike, and the forward-combed hair of her initiates remains, in Thompson's phrase, a liturgy anyone can read: everyone who has dressed carefully on a difficult morning knows her rite. The quiet one, her cult insists, was the permanent one all along.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọba is the goddess of what remains when the shouting is over. The storm-wives got the thunder; she got the river — and rivers outlive storms by definition. Her crown covers her ear, not her shame: the difference is everything. She asks the question the senior wife knows best: after the injustice, what do you cover, what do you keep, and what do you let become a lake?

The priests say her crown was made to her own design, after the flight — the first piece of regalia in the corpus that exists to hide a wound and to honor it at once. The river does not hide; it covers, and continues. Reconciliation is not mandatory in her tellings, but endurance is possible, and her lake holds its annual mourners quietly, without demanding anyone forgive.

lore.archaeology: Her river rises in the hills of the Ọyọ country, and her cult-centers at Ọṣogbo and the Ọba lake preserve her shrines and her priests; the brass and terracotta figures of the covered-ear goddess are documented in museum collections from Ifẹ̀ to Havana. The oríkì of the three wives, recorded by Bascom and others, is among the finest domestic myth-cycles in the Yoruba corpus — an archive kept not in stone but in living recitation, which is precisely the kind of evidence this tradition chose to leave.
